data.title: Light-induced targeting enables proteomics on endogenous condensates
data.projectDescription: Endogenous condensates with transient constituents are notoriously difficult to study with common biological assays like mass-spectrometry and other proteomics profiling. Here we report a method for light-induced targeting of endogenous condensates (LiTEC) in living cells. LiTEC combines the identification of molecular zip codes that target the endogenous condensates with optogenetics to enable controlled and reversible partitioning of an arbitrary cargo, such as enzymes commonly used in proteomics, into the condensate in a blue light dependent manner. We demonstrate a proof of concept by combining LiTEC with proximity-based biotinylation (BioID) and uncover putative components of transcriptional condensates in mouse embryonic stem cells. Our approach opens the road to genome-wide functional studies of endogenous condensates.
data.sampleProcessingProtocol: Cell culture Transgene expression was induced by addition of doxycycline. Extra biotin (final concentration 500 μM) was directly added to cells 30 min prior to  blue light LED illumination (30 min with 3.42 mW/cm2 on average, 465 nm peak)). After 30 min incubation with/without blue light, 2i media with/without Dox or extra biotin were immediately discarded prior nuclear extract (NE) preparation. Streptavidin pull-down mESC NEs were prepared employing Buffer C according to the Dignam protocol.  First, 40 µl of Streptavidin-beads were put into two Mobicol tubes, respectively and washed with 250 µl ice-cold Buffer C Complete (Buffer C + 0.2% NP40) for 1 min, followed by centrifugation. This step was repeated twice and 600 µl Buffer C Complete was added to one tube (biotin-free bead or “Bead”) whereas 600 µl Buffer C Complete containing 1 mM biotin was added to the other tube (biotin-blocked bead or “Block”), followed by incubation at 4°C for 60 min.  Beads were centrifuged and washed four times with ice-cold 600 µl Buffer C. After spinning down and discarding the supernatant, 400 µl Buffer C was added to each tube and 100 µl per tube were transferred to three new tubes (in total, three “Bead” tubes + three “Block” tubes). 1 mg of NE was added to new tubes and the total volume of each tube was adjusted to 600 µl with Buffer C, followed by incubation at 4°C room for 75 min.  After incubation, beads were centrifuged and the supernatants were discarded. Beads were washed twice with three different buffers as described in the following (total 6 times). First, 600 µl ice-cold Buffer C was admixed twice. Then 600 µl ice-cold 1x PBS  (+ 0.5% NP40) was added twice, and finally 600 µl ice-cold neat 1x PBS was applied twice for washing.  On-bead digestion Streptavidin beads were washed once in 100 µl 100 mM Tris pH 7.5, 0.02% Rapigest and transferred to fresh 1.5 ml low bind tubes. After centrifugation and removal of the supernatant, beads were resuspended in 50 µl on-bead digestion buffer containing 2 M Urea , 200 mM EPPS, pH 8.25, 8% Acetonitrile (ACN). Samples were reduced by addition of TCEP  to a final concentration of 10 mM  and alkylated by adding 2-chloroacetamide  to a final concentration of 40 mM. For protein digestion, 250 ng Lys-C (Wako) was added and the samples were incubated for 3 hours at 28°C. Following a 1:2 dilution with HPLC grade water and the addition of 240 ng trypsin (Promega), the samples were incubated overnight at 25°C. To collect tryptic peptides, beads were spun down, and the supernatant was transferred to a fresh 1.5 ml low bind tube. Beads were washed once with 50 µl HPLC grade water, and the supernatants were combined and acidified by the addition of TFA to a final concentration of 1%. 50 µl 0.5%  acetic acid and 0.02% HFBA were added to each sample (ACN concentration <2%).  LC-MS STAGEtip purification was carried out according to Rappsilber et al. Peptides were eluted with 40 µl of 0.1% FA/80%  ACN  and concentrated to a volume of 2 µl in a vacuum evaporator followed by the addition of 1.5 µl 1% TFA/5%  ACN. Finally, the total volume was adjusted to 10 µl with 0.1% FA. LC-MS/MS analysis were performed on an Exploris 480 MS coupled to a nLC1200. Separation of peptides was performed at 30°C on in-house packed fused-silica emitter microcolumns (75 µm ID, 8 µm tip, 50 cm length filled with ReproSil-Pur 120 C18-AQ beads (Dr. Maisch). Peptides were separated using a binary solvent system consisting of 0.1% FA (solvent A) and 80% ACN/ 0.1% FA (solvent B). Peptides were loaded at 0% B and then separated by the following linear gradients: from 0% to 8% solvent B over 5 min at 250 nl/min, from 8% to 35% over 40 min at 250 nl/min, from 35% to 80% over 4 min at 350 nl/min, and kept at 80% for 5 min at 500 nl/min followed by an inverse gradient from 80% to 2% over 2 min and a re-equilibration step over 5 min at 0 % B (500 nl/min). For DDA acquisition, we utilized the “fast” and “sensitive” methods (Musa et al., 2018) with the following alterations: the full scan spectra were acquired at m/z 300-1650 with 60 000 resolution. Target values were set to 2.0e5 or 8.0e4, RF lens at 40% or 45%, and maximum injection time at 45 ms or 60 ms, for “fast” and “sensitive” modes, respectively. The 20 most intense multiply charged ions (z = 2-6) were sequentially isolated and fragmented by higher-energy collisional dissociation (HCD) with max. injection time of 22 ms and 7500 resolution for the “fast”, or with max. injection time of 50 ms and 15000 resolution for the “sensitive” acquisition method. Spray voltage was at +2.1 kV, normalized HCD collision energy (NCE) at 30%, dynamic exclusion time at 30 s, and isolation window at 1.5 m/z.
data.dataProcessingProtocol:
MS data processing with Max Quant:  
Raw files of LC-MS/MS analyses were processed together employing MaxQuant (Cox et al., 2008), version 2.3.10. For peptide identification spectra were matched against the mus musculus Uniprot FASTA database (including isoforms, release 08.03.2023, 63.762 entries), to which the sequences of transgenically expressed proteins, namely BRD4IDR-mCh-sspB, scFv-sfGFP-iLID and mTurboID-24xSunTag were added, and a common in-house curated contaminants FASTA file using the Andromeda (Cox et al., 2011) search engine embedded in MaxQuant. Cysteine carbamidomethylation was set as a fixed modification and N-terminal acetylation, methionine oxidation, and deamidation at asparagine or glutamine as variable modifications with deamidation at asparagine or glutamine excluded within the “First search” option. The enzyme specificity was set to trypsin/P (enabling cleavage before proline) and a maximum of two missed cleavages were allowed. The minimum peptide length was set to 6 amino acids. A false discovery rate of 1% was applied to both peptide and protein lists using the decoy mode “Revert.” The option “Match between runs” was enabled for sample batches that were measured employing  the same column with a retention time window setting of 0.5 min. Label-free quantification (LFQ) and intensity-based absolute quantification (iBAQ) were enabled. At least one unique peptide was required for identification and quantification. 

MS data processing using FragPipe:
Raw files were reprocessed with FragPipe (Kong et al., 2017; doi: 10.1038/nmeth.4256) version 22.016 defining them as DDA+ type (full isolation window search) and using the LFQ-MBR workflow with default values unless stated. Searching was done against the same aforementioned database, concatenating equal contaminants together with an in-software-generated decoy database. Precursor mass error was set to ± 30 ppm, identical fixed and variable modifications as with MaxQuant were employed and stricttrypsin (up to 2 miss cleavages) was set as enzyme. MSBooster re-scoring was activated, peptide-spectrum matches were validated with Percolator and protein inference was done with ProteinProphet. Quantification was done with IonQuant using match-between runs with ion FDR ≤ 0.01, minimum correlation 0.2, and top runs 100. 

Proteomics data analysis:
For downstream data analysis, an in-house developed R package/Shiny App App assembled from extensive R functions built around the DEP package (Love, M. et al., 2017. DESeq2 (Bioconductor), DOI: 10.18129/B9.bioc.DESeq2) was employed. Briefly, for MaxQuant results reverse, contaminants, only identified by site entries were removed as well as proteins with less than 2 quantified peptides. Downstream analysis was done on protein groups with at least 60% valid values in a condition across all replicates. Missing values were imputed if completely absent or if less than 2 values were present per condition using a left-censor strategy (width = 0.4, shift = 1.2) as described before (Keilhauer et al., 2015;  DOI: 10.1074/mcp.M114.041012 ). 
FragPipe results were filtered for contaminants and decoy entries. An experimental design was used in which the condition “ALL” was set as target and the rest of the conditions were treated as general background as described (Keilhauer et al., 2015). For downstream analysis, only protein groups with at least 60% valid values in the “ALL” condition were considered. Missing values were imputed using a mixed strategy. If completely absent or missing in more than 60% per condition using a left-censor strategy (width = 0.3, shift = 1.8) and the remaining using the missForest random forest approach (Stekhoven et al., 2012; https://doi.org/10.1093/bioinformatics/btr597). 
Statistical analysis was done by fitting a linear model using limma (Ritchie et al., 2015;  doi: 10.1093/nar/gkv007) (with trend=TRUE) for both software pipelines, but for FragPipe results, a batch effect was included in the model for the first and second replicates in all conditions/replicates as determined by quality-control evaluation. Obtained p-values were corrected for multiple hypothesis testing by Benjamini-Hochberg (Benjamini and Hochberg, 1995;  https://doi.org/10.1111/j.2517-6161.1995.tb02031.x) procedure. Differentially enriched proteins were classified by having a fold change of ± 2 (non-log) condition vs control and a p-value ≤ 0.05.
